Surah al-Ra'd (The Thunder)

It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir, and Madani according to al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is Madani except for two verses from it, and they are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved...﴾ to the end of the two.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book.﴾ Regarding "the Book" there are three opinions:

First: the Zabur (Psalms), this is the saying of Matar.

Second: the Torah and the Gospel, said by Mujahid.

Third: the Qur'an, said by Qatadah.

According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ means: these are the verses of the Book.

﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾ means the Qur'an.

﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾ means: they do not believe in the Qur'an, that it was sent down with the truth.

Regarding the intended meaning of ﴿most of the people﴾ there are two opinions:

One: most of the Jews and Christians, because most of them did not embrace Islam.

Second: most of the people during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 2:

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Allah is the One who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: it means, with pillars that you cannot see. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they are raised without any pillars. This was said by Qatadah and Iyas ibn Muawiyah.

As for the raising of the heaven, there are two aspects. The first: the raising of its rank and the magnification of its worth, because the heaven is more noble than the earth.

The second: its height, so that it rose above the earth.

؎ I love Him, and by He who set firm its foundations, a love which, when His signs appear, hides them.

وَفِيهِ وجْهانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنْ يَتَّصِلَ ما يَكُونُ نَباتُهُ مُرًّا.

"The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾ — the verse.

Its meaning: And if you, O Muhammad, are amazed at their denial of you, then more amazing than that is their denial of the Resurrection.

Allah, exalted is He, does not feel amazement (ta'ajjub), and it is not permissible for Him to be characterized by it, because it is a change in the self caused by hidden causes. He only mentioned it so that His Prophet and the believers would be amazed at it."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 6:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: they mean the punishment before the well-being (al-'afiyah). This was said by Qatadah.

The second: [they mean] the evil before the good. This is a statement narrated by Sa'id ibn Bashir.

The third: [they mean] disbelief before the response (al-ijabah).

This was narrated by al-Qasim ibn Yahya.

And it may bear a fourth meaning: [they mean] fighting before seeking guidance (al-istirshad).

﴿And exemplary punishments (al-mathulat) have already passed away before them﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: the examples (al-amthal) which Allah, exalted is He, set forth for them. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they are the punishments through which Allah, exalted is He, made examples of the earlier nations. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they are the uprooting punishments which leave nothing remaining, such as the punishments of 'Ad and Thamud. This is related by Ibn al-Anbari. The word al-mathulat is the plural of mathulah.

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: He forgives them their past wrongdoing by their repentance in the present. This was said by al-Qasim ibn Yahya.

The second: He forgives them by pardoning them from hastening the punishment, despite their wrongdoing in hastening sin.

The third: He forgives them by granting them respite, in anticipation of their repentance.

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said upon the revelation of this verse: "Were it not for Allah's pardon and His overlooking, no one would enjoy life. And were it not for His warning and His punishment, everyone would become complacent."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 7:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, you are only a warner﴾, means: the Prophet (ﷺ) is a warner to his community. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾. Concerning this there are six interpretations.

The first: "a guide" refers to Allah Most High. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, meaning a prophet who guides them. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The third: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, its meaning being that for every people there are leaders and guides. This was said by Abu Salih.

The fourth: ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, meaning callers (duʿat) to the truth. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: its meaning is that for every people there is a deed (ʿamal). This was said by Abu al-ʿAliyah.

The sixth: its meaning is that for every people there is one who precedes them with knowledge, leading them to guidance. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verses 8–9:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾. Ibn Abi Najih said: He knows whether it is male or female.

It may also carry another meaning: He knows whether it is righteous or wicked.

﴿And what the wombs fall short of and what they increase﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations:

The first: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to an incomplete miscarriage, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to a complete child. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.

The second: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to delivery before nine months, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to delivery after nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

Al-Dahhak said: My mother bore me while carrying me in her womb for two years, and she gave birth to me when my teeth had already come out.

The third: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the cessation of menstruation during pregnancy, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to postpartum bleeding (nifas) after delivery.

Makhul said: God, exalted is He, made menstrual blood a nourishment for the fetus.

The fourth: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the appearance of menstruation for some days during pregnancy, and in that there is a deficiency in the child. ﴿What they increase﴾ refers to the days of pregnancy that correspond to the days of menstruation, because whenever she menstruates for a day during her pregnancy, she gains a day of purity, until her pregnancy completes nine months in purity. This was said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The fifth: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the one whom they bore before, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to the one they will bear afterward. This was related by al-Suddi and Qatadah.

﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it refers to provision and term of life. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it refers to what the wombs fall short of and what they increase. This was said by al-Dahhak.

It may also carry a third meaning: that everything with Him, of reward and punishment, is in measure with obedience and disobedience.

The second: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to delivery before nine months, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to delivery after nine months. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

Al-Dahhak said: My mother bore me while carrying me in her womb for two years, and she gave birth to me when my teeth had already come out.

The third: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the cessation of menstruation during pregnancy, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to postpartum bleeding (nifas) after delivery.

Makhul said: God, exalted is He, made menstrual blood a nourishment for the fetus.

The fourth: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the appearance of menstruation for some days during pregnancy, and in that there is a deficiency in the child. ﴿What they increase﴾ refers to the days of pregnancy that correspond to the days of menstruation, because whenever she menstruates for a day during her pregnancy, she gains a day of purity, until her pregnancy completes nine months in purity. This was said by Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The fifth: ﴿what the wombs fall short of﴾ refers to the one whom they bore before, and ﴿what they increase﴾ refers to the one they will bear afterward. This was related by al-Suddi and Qatadah.

﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: it refers to provision and term of life. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it refers to what the wombs fall short of and what they increase. This was said by al-Dahhak.

It may also carry a third meaning: that everything with Him, of reward and punishment, is in measure with obedience and disobedience.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verses 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or speaks aloud with it.﴾ Concealing speech (*israr al-qawl*) is what a person says to himself, and speaking aloud (*al-jahr*) is what he says to others.

The meaning is that He, may He be exalted, knows what a person conceals of good and evil.

﴿And whoever hides by night and goes forth freely by day.﴾ On this there are two views. The first: He knows the one who hides his deed in the darkness of night and the one who displays it in the light of day.

The second: He sees what the darkness of night conceals just as He sees what the light of day reveals, unlike created beings, for whom the night conceals the conditions of their families.

The poet said:

"And a night, of which people say, in its darkness, that the sound-eyed and the blind are alike."

*Al-sarib* is the one who departs and goes away, derived from *al-surub* in pasture, which is in the evening, while *al-suruh* is in the morning. Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"Where have you wandered, though you were not one who wanders? And dreams bring near what is not near."

His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿For him there are successive angels (*mu'aqqibat*) before him and behind him.﴾ *Mu'aqqibat* is a term for those who follow one another in succession. On this there are three opinions:

The first: they are the guards of rulers who take turns in guarding. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah.

The second: they are what follows one another of the commands of God and His decree concerning His servants. This was said by Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The third: they are the angels. When the angels of the day ascend, the angels of the night follow them, and when the angels of the night ascend, the angels of the day follow them. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

Al-Hasan said: they are four angels, two by day and two by night, who gather at the time of the dawn prayer.

As for His saying, ﴿before him and behind him,﴾ there are three meanings. The first: in front of him and behind him. This is the view of those who held that the *mu'aqqibat* are the guards of rulers.

The second: the past and the future. This is the view of those who held that the *mu'aqqibat* are what follows one another from the command and decree of God, may He be exalted.

The third: from his guidance and his misguidance. This is the view of those who held that the *mu'aqqibat* are the angels.

﴿They guard him by the command of God.﴾ Its interpretation varies according to the differing views on the *mu'aqqibat*. If it is said, according to the first view, that they are the guards of rulers, then in His saying ﴿they guard him﴾ the meaning is: in his presence, by the command of God, and none can repel His command or avert His decree. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ikrimah.

The second: there is an implied negative particle in the sentence, and its sense is: they do not guard him from the command of God.

If it is said, according to the second view, that the *mu'aqqibat* are what follows one another of the command of God and His decree, then in the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿they guard him from the command of God,﴾ there are two meanings. The first: they guard him from death, as long as his term has not come. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: they guard him from jinn and harmful vermin, as long as no decree has come. This was said by Abu Malik and Ka'b al-Ahbar.

If it is said, according to the third view, which is the most likely, that the *mu'aqqibat* are the angels, then concerning what is meant by their guarding him there are two meanings. The first: they guard his good deeds and his bad deeds by the command of God. The second: they guard his person.

On this basis, in the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿they guard him from the command of God,﴾ there are three meanings. The first: they guard him by the command of God. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: they guard him from the command of God until the command of God comes. This is reported from Ibn Abbas.

The third: the sentence is inverted, and its sense is: for him there are successive angels of the command of God, may He be exalted, who guard him before him and behind him. This was said by Ibrahim.

Concerning this verse there are two views. The first: it is general, applying to all creation. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is specific, and was revealed concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, the brother of Labid, resolved to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God, may He be mighty and majestic, protected him from both of them and revealed this verse concerning him. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿Indeed God does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves.﴾ This may bear two meanings. The first: God does not change a blessing from a people until they change what is in themselves of disobedience.

The second: He does not change what is with them of blessing until they change what is in themselves of obedience.

﴿And when God wills evil for a people, there is no turning it back.﴾ On this there are two meanings:

The first: when God wills punishment for them, there is no turning back of His punishment.

The second: when He wills for them a trial of illnesses and sicknesses, there is no turning back of His trial.

﴿And they have besides Him no protector.﴾ On this there are two meanings: (p. 100) The first: no refuge, which is the meaning of the saying of al-Suddi.

The second: that is, no helper. From this is the saying of the poet:

"There is nothing in the heaven besides the Merciful who is a protector."

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 13, verses 12–13:

His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: a fear for the traveler of its harm, and a hope for the resident of its blessing. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: a fear of the thunderbolts of lightning, and a hope for its rain which removes drought. This was said by al-Hasan.

It has been reported that "the Prophet (ﷺ), when he heard the sound of thunder, would say: 'O Allah, do not kill us by Your anger, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that.'"

The third: a fear of His punishment and a hope for His reward.

﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾. Mujahid said: "Heavy with water."

His saying, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Regarding the thunder there are two views. The first: it is the audible sound. It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Thunder is a warning from Allah, so when you hear it, refrain from sins."

The second: the thunder is an angel, and the audible sound is its glorification. This was said by Ikrimah.

﴿And the angels, out of awe of Him﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: the angels glorify Allah out of awe of Allah, the Exalted. This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The second: out of awe of the thunder, and this is perhaps the view of Mujahid.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾. There is disagreement about who this was revealed concerning, and there are three statements. The first: it was revealed concerning a man who denied the Qur'an and denied the Prophet (ﷺ), and a thunderbolt seized him. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it was revealed concerning Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, who had intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) together with Amir ibn al-Tufayl, but his hand became stiff upon his sword, and Allah the Exalted protected him from both of them. Then he departed, and Allah the Exalted sent upon him a thunderbolt that burned him.

Ibn Jarir said: Concerning this his brother Labid says:

"I fear for Arbad the calamities of death, and I do not dread the rising of the Simak or the Asad stars.
The lightning and the thunderbolts struck him, along with the cavalry, on the day of the noble, valiant ones."

The third: it was revealed concerning a Jew who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Tell me about your Lord, of what is He made? Of pearl or of ruby?" Then a thunderbolt came and seized him. This was said by Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid.

Aban related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The thunderbolt does not seize one who remembers Allah, may He be mighty and majestic."

﴿While they dispute about Allah﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it refers to the dispute of the Jew when he asked about Allah: "Of what is He?" This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the dispute of Arbad concerning what he intended of killing the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And He is severe in might﴾. Regarding this there are nine interpretations. The first: meaning severe in enmity. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: severe in malice. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: severe in strength. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: severe in anger. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fifth: severe in stratagem. This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The sixth: severe in power. This was also said by Ibn Abbas.

The seventh: severe in destruction through famine, which is drought. This was also said by al-Hasan.

The eighth: severe in seizing. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The ninth: severe in retribution and punishment. This was said by Abu Ubaydah, who recited for A'sha of Banu Tha'labah:

"A branch of a tree swaying on the bough of glory, generous in giving, great in might."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He, ﴿To Him is the true call﴾, has three interpretations. The first: the true call is "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh); this is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: Allah Exalted is Himself the Truth (al-Ḥaqq), so calling upon Him is the call of the Truth.

The third: sincerity (al-ikhlāṣ) in supplication is the true call; this was said by some of the later scholars (mutaʾakhkhirīn).

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that the true call is supplication to Him at the time of fear, because in that state none is called upon except Him, as Allah Exalted says, ﴿Those whom you call upon fail you except Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67]. This is more fitting to the context of the verse, because He said, ﴿And those who call upon other than Him﴾, meaning the idols and the images.

﴿They do not respond to them with anything﴾, that is, they do not answer their supplication, nor do they hear their call.

﴿Like one who stretches out his hands toward water to make it reach his mouth, but it will not reach it﴾. Allah Exalted has struck the water as a parable for their despair of their supplication being answered, because the Arabs use as a proverb for one who strives after what he cannot attain the image of one who grasps water with the hand, as Abu al-Hudhayl said:

﴾ So I have become, regarding what was between me and her of affection, like one who grasps water in his hand.

There are three aspects to the meaning of this parable. The first: the one who calls upon a god other than Allah is like the thirsty man who calls for water to reach his mouth from afar, wishing to take it, yet cannot reach it with his tongue, and he gestures toward it with his hand, but it never comes to him; for the water does not respond to him, and the water does not reach him. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: he is like the thirsty man who sees his reflection in the water, having extended his palm into it so that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach him, because his assumption is false and his imagining is corrupt. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: he is like one who stretches his hand to the water to grasp it, but nothing from it remains in his two palms.

Al-Farraʾ claimed that what is meant by the water here is the well (al-biʾr), because it is the source (maʿdin) of water, and that the parable is like one who extends his hand to the well without a rope (rishāʾ). Its witness is the poet's saying:

﴾ Indeed the water is the water of my father and my grandfather, * and the well: I dug it and I cleared it out.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿To Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations.

The first: "willingly" refers to the prostration of the believer, and "unwillingly" to the prostration of the disbeliever. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "willingly" refers to whoever entered Islam out of desire, and "unwillingly" to whoever entered it out of fear, by the sword. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: "willingly" refers to whoever has been in Islam for a long period so that he has grown accustomed to prostration, and "unwillingly" to whoever has only just begun Islam until he becomes accustomed to prostration. This was related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: what was said by some of the people of spiritual insights (ashab al-khawatir), that when calamities befall a person he becomes humbled, and when blessings follow one another upon him he becomes weary.

﴿And their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings﴾. He means that the shadow of every person prostrates along with his prostration: the shadow of the believer prostrates willingly, just as the prostration of the believer is willing, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly, just as the prostration of the disbeliever is unwilling.

Al-Asal (the evenings) is the plural of asul, and asul is the plural of asil. Al-Asil is al-ashiyy (the late afternoon), which is the period between the afternoon prayer (al-asr) and sunset (al-maghrib). Abu Dhu'ayb said:

By my life, you are indeed the house most noble of its people,
and the one who sits most in its shades during the evenings.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 16:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to say to the polytheists of Quraysh: ﴿Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ Then He commanded him to say to them: ﴿Say: Allah.﴾ If they did not say this, it was for the sake of making it understood, and they said it as an affirmation, because He made it a binding argument (ilzam).

﴿Say: Have you then taken besides Him protectors who do not control for themselves any benefit or harm?﴾ Then He commanded him, peace and blessings be upon him, to say this to them after their acknowledgment of Allah: Have you then taken, besides the Creator, the Bestower of favours, gods of idols and images, and worshipped them besides Him, which do not control for themselves any benefit that they could convey to them, nor any harm that they could ward off from them? So how could they control for you any benefit or harm? And this is a sound argument (ilzam).

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing alike? Or are the darknesses and the light alike?﴾ This is a parable which Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever: the blind and the seeing are like them, and guidance and error are like the darknesses and the light. The believer, in his guidance, is like the seeing one who walks in the light, and the disbeliever, in his error, is like the blind one who walks in the darknesses. The two are not alike, so likewise the believer and the disbeliever are not alike. This is among the most sound parables Allah the Exalted has struck and the clearest of comparisons.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created as He creates, so that the creation became confused to them?﴾ Its meaning: since their gods which they worshipped did not create a creation like the creation of Allah, so that the creation of their gods would resemble the creation of Allah to them, why then did it become confused to them, to the point that they worshipped them as the worship of Allah the Exalted? ﴿Say: Allah is the Creator of everything.﴾ Thus it follows from this that everything must worship Him.

﴿And He is the One, the Subduer.﴾ In His saying ﴿so that the creation became confused to them﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: so that the creation became alike to them (fa-tamathala). The second: so that the creation became unclear to them (fa-ashkala). Ibn Shajara mentioned both of them.

The Exalted said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it means according to what He has ordained for them, whether little or much.

The second: it means that the small of the valleys flows according to its smallness, and the large of them flows according to its largeness.

This is a parable which Allah the Exalted struck for the Qur'an and what enters the hearts from it. He likened the Qur'an to rain, because of the generality of its good and the lastingness of its benefit, and He likened the hearts to valleys: into them enters of the Qur'an what enters the valleys of water, according to their breadth and narrowness.

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, i.e., the Qur'an; ﴿and valleys flow according to their capacity﴾. He said: "The valleys are the hearts of the servants."

﴿So the torrent carries a swelling foam﴾. Rabin (swelling): that which is raised up high.

This is a parable which Allah the Exalted struck for truth and falsehood: truth is represented by the water that remains in the earth so that benefit is derived from it, and falsehood is represented by the foam that goes off as scum and from which no benefit is derived.

Then He struck a second parable with fire, saying: ﴿And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament﴾, meaning gold and silver;

﴿or goods﴾, meaning brass and copper;

﴿there is a scum like it﴾, meaning that when it is smelted in the fire it has a dross like the foam on the water, which goes away and from which no benefit is derived, like falsehood; and what remains pure is the essence from which benefit is derived, like truth.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then it goes away as scum﴾, there are three interpretations concerning it. The first: it means "split apart," as said by Ibn Jarir.

The second: "floating on the surface of the earth," as said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: "cast away," as said by Ibn Ishaq.

Abu 'Ubayda related that he heard Ru'ba recite: "jifalan" (جِفالًا).

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said "ajfalat al-qidr" (أجفلت القدر) when the cooking pot casts out its foam.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿For those who respond to their Lord is the best (reward)﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is Paradise, related by Ubayy ibn Ka'b from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It may also bear a third interpretation: that it refers to the multiplication of good deeds.

The third: it is rebuke and reproach, related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The fourth: it is that their good deeds will not be accepted, so their evil deeds will not be forgiven.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: that "the evil of the reckoning" is the evil to which their reckoning leads, namely punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 28–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾. In it there are four interpretations:

First: "In the remembrance of Allah" means with their mouths. This was said by Qatadah.

Second: "With the blessing of Allah upon them."

Third: "With the promise of Allah to them." This was mentioned by Ibn ʿIsa.

Fourth: "With the Qur'an." This was said by Mujahid.

﴿Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ may bear three interpretations:

First: "In the remembrance of Allah" means in obedience to Allah.

Second: in the reward of Allah.

Third: in the promise of Allah to them, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is ṭūbā (a good state, or a tree in Paradise) and a good place of return﴾. In it there are nine interpretations:

First: that ṭūbā is one of the names of Paradise. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: the meaning of "ṭūbā for them" is "ḥusnā for them." This was said by Qatadah.

Third: its meaning is "how excellent is what is theirs." This was said by ʿIkrimah.

Fourth: its meaning is "good for them." This was said by Ibrahim.

Fifth: its meaning is "a delight for them." This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥak.

Sixth: its meaning is "joy and coolness of the eye for them." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Seventh: "the good life for them." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Eighth: that ṭūbā is on the pattern fuʿlā from al-ṭayyib (goodness), as it is said "afḍal" and "fuḍlā." This was mentioned by Ibn ʿIsa.

Most of these meanings are close to one another.

Regarding the word itself there are three opinions: First: that it is an Ethiopian word. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: that it is an Indian word. This was said by ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud.

Third: that it is an Arabic word. This was said by the majority (al-Jumhur).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: He is my Lord﴾. Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that the treaty between him and them be written down. He said to the scribe: (Write, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"). They said: "We do not know what al-Rahman is; write only: 'In Your name, O Allah.'"

It is related from Ibn Ishaq that they said: "It has reached us that what teaches you this that you bring is a man from the people of al-Yamamah called al-Rahman, and by Allah, we will never believe in him ever." So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: He is my Lord; there is no god but He﴾, meaning that He is one God, even though His names differ.

﴿In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return﴾. Mujahid said: by al-matab (return) is meant repentance.

A second possible meaning: "and to Him is the place of return."(p-112)

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion, or the earth were split asunder...﴾ to the end of the verse.

The cause of its revelation is what Mujahid and Qatadah related: the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you would like us to follow you, then move our mountains away from us so that our land may become wider for us, for it is narrow. Bring the Levant (al-Sham) close to us, for we trade there. And bring the dead out of their graves so that we may speak with them." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which the mountains were set in motion﴾, meaning, were removed far away.

﴿Or the earth were split asunder﴾, meaning, were brought near.

﴿Or the dead were made to speak﴾, meaning, were brought back to life.

The answer to this is omitted, and its estimated form is: "This Qur'an would have been [this one]." It was omitted for brevity, because the apparent meaning of the speech already indicates the implied omitted element.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, the affair belongs entirely to Allah﴾, meaning, He is the Owner of all affairs, and He does what He wills of them.

﴿Have not those who believe despaired, that if Allah willed, He would have guided all the people?﴾ This is because when the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what they asked, the believers were uneasy about it, so Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired﴾. In this there are three interpretations.

The first: its meaning is "Have not those who believe become certain (yatabayyan)?" This was said by 'Atiyyah. In the first recitation (qira'ah) it reads: "Have not those who believe become certain?"

It is also said that in the dialect of Jurhum, ﴿yay'as﴾ means "yatabayyan," that is, "become certain."

The second: "Have not those who believe known (ya'lam)?" This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. From it is the verse of Rabah ibn 'Adiyy:

"Did not the people know (yay'as) that I am his son, even though I am far from the land of my tribe?"

The third: "Have not those who believe despaired, by their hopes being cut off?"

Regarding what they despaired of, according to this interpretation, there are two views. The first: they despaired of what the polytheists asked for; this was said by al-Farra'.

The second: they despaired that these polytheists would believe; this was said by al-Kisa'i.

﴿That if Allah willed, He would have guided all the people﴾. In this there are two views. The first: He would have guided them to faith. The second: He would have guided them to Paradise.

﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve for what they have done, or it will settle close to their homes﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: what strikes them of punishment and affliction; this was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jarir.

The second: that it refers to the advance raiding parties and expeditions that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to dispatch; this was said by 'Ikrimah.

﴿Or it will settle close to their homes﴾. In this there are two views. The first: "or the disaster will settle close to their homes"; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: "or you, O Muhammad, will settle close to their homes"; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

﴿Until the promise of Allah comes﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: the conquest of Makkah; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the Resurrection; this was said by al-Hasan.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verses 32–33:**

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Is He who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: they are the angels who were assigned to the children of Adam, as said by al-Dahhak.

The second: it is Allah, who stands over every soul in what it has earned, as said by Qatadah.

The third: it refers to Himself.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿qa'im﴾ (standing), there are two interpretations. The first: it means *wali* (governing, in charge), as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿standing in justice﴾, meaning governing with justice.

The second: it means knowing what it has earned. The poet said:

> Were it not for men of Quraysh, noble and mighty, you would have stolen the garments of the House, and Allah is watching (*qa'im*).

The phrase ﴿in what it has earned﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: what it has earned of provision, as a favour bestowed upon it, so that it comes in the sense of reminding of blessings. The second: what it has earned of deeds, as a guarding over it, so that it comes in the sense of promise and warning.

﴿And they set up for Allah partners﴾, meaning idols they made into gods.

﴿Say: name them﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: say, name them as gods, in the manner of a threat. The second: meaning, describe them, so that they may know that they cannot be gods.

﴿Or will you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth﴾, meaning: will you inform Him of what He does not know, that there is in the earth a god other than Him?

﴿Or with an outward saying﴾ has four interpretations. The first: its meaning is with falsehood of speech, as said by Qatadah, and from it is the poet's saying:

> You reproached us for their milk and their meat, and that is a disgrace, O son of Rayta, evident.

(p-١١٥) That is, with an unfounded claim.

The second: with a conjecture of speech, which is the view of Mujahid.

The third: with a lie of speech, as said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that the outward speech is the Qur'an, as said by al-Suddi.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: that the outward speech is a proof which they display by their words, and the meaning of the statement is: will you inform Him of that as witnesses, or will you speak as those who argue?

**The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 13, verses 34–35:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it is a comparison for the Garden (al-Jannah). This was said by Ali ibn Isa.

The second: it is a description (na't) of the Garden, because the Garden has no like. This was said by Ikrimah.

﴿Beneath it rivers flow; its food is everlasting﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: its fruit is not cut off. This was said by al-Qasim ibn Yahya.

The second: its pleasure in the mouths remains. This was said by Ibrahim al-Taymi.

And it may bear a third meaning: it does not cause boredom to one who is satisfied, nor is there any mirbad (a thing that causes hunger or stops it) for one who is hungry.

﴿And its shade﴾ may bear two aspects. The first: it is everlasting in continuance.

(p-١١٦) The second: it is everlasting in pleasure.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verses 36–37:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book rejoice in what has been sent down to you﴾. Concerning them there are three opinions:

First: they are the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who rejoiced in what was sent down to him of the Qur'an. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

Second: they are the believers among the People of the Book. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: they are the People of the Book from among the Jews and Christians who rejoiced in what was sent down to him concerning the confirmation of their Scriptures. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions:

One: they are the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Second: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Concerning their denial of part of it there are two aspects:

One: they recognised the description (naʿt) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in their Scriptures, yet denied his prophethood.

Second: they recognised his truthfulness, yet denied that they should confirm it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verse 38–39:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾. By "wives" he means women, and by "offspring" he means children.

There are two interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is that the messengers We sent before you were human beings who had wives and offspring like all other humans, so why did they deny your message when you are like those who came before you?

The second: He forbade him thereby from celibacy (tabattul), as said by Qatadah.

It is also said that the Jews criticized the Prophet ﷺ for having wives, so God Most High sent down concerning them, teaching them that this is the custom of the messengers before him.

﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾. It is said that the polytheists of Quraysh asked him for signs, some of which have already been mentioned in this surah, so God Most High sent down this verse concerning them.

﴿For every term there is a Book﴾. There are three interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is that for every Book sent down from heaven there is a term (ajal).

This is from the front-and-back (al-muqaddam wal-mu'akhkhar, i.e., inversion of order in the verse), as said by al-Dahhak.

The second: its meaning is that for every matter decreed by God Most High there is a Book in which He has written it, as said by Ibn Jarir.

The third: for every term (ajal) of the creatures there is a Book with God Most High, as said by al-Hasan.

It may also admit a fourth: for every deed there is a report.

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and confirms﴾. There are seven interpretations of this. The first: Allah effaces what He wills of the affairs of His servants and changes it, except for wretchedness and happiness, for these are not changed, as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: Allah effaces what He wills and confirms what He wills in a Book other than the Mother of the Book. There are two books: one of them is the Mother of the Book, which He does not change, nor does He erase anything from it as He wishes, as said by Ikrimah.

(p-118) The third: that Mighty and Majestic God abrogates what He wills of the rulings of His Book and confirms what He wills of them, so it is not abrogated, as said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: that He effaces whoever's term has come and confirms whoever's term has not come, as said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: He forgives what He wills of the sins of His servants and leaves what He wills so He does not forgive it, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The sixth: that it is the man who puts forward obedience and then ends it with disobedience, so that erases what has preceded, and the man who puts forward disobedience and then ends it with obedience, so that erases what has preceded. This view is also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.

The seventh: that the recording angels (al-hafazah) from among the angels raise up all his words and deeds, so Allah Mighty and Majestic erases from them what contains no reward or punishment and confirms what contains reward and punishment, as said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾. There are six interpretations of this. The first: it is the lawful and the unlawful, as said by al-Hasan.

The second: the totality of the Book, as said by al-Dahhak.

The third: it is Allah Most High's knowledge of what He created and what He will create, as said by Ka'b al-Ahbar.

The fourth: it is the Reminder (al-dhikr), as said by Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: that it is the Book which is not altered, as said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: that it is the origin of the Book in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), as said by Ikrimah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 13, verses 42–43:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger."﴾ Qatadah said: They are the polytheists of the Arabs.

﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you."﴾ That is, He testifies to my truthfulness and your falsehood.

﴿And [with] whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ — concerning this there are three opinions. The first: they are ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Salman, and Tamim al-Dari; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: it is Jibril (Gabriel); this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: it is Allah, the Exalted; this was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak.

They used to recite ﴿وَمَن عِنْدَهُ عِلْمُ الكِتابِ﴾ (wa-man ʿindahu ʿilm al-kitab), meaning: "min ʿind Allah ʿilm al-kitab" (the knowledge of the Book is from Allah), and they would deny the one who said it refers to ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and Salman, because they held that the surah is Meccan, while these two embraced Islam in Medina. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best what is correct.
